text: Lesson 2 decided the fact table will carry keys only, not names. But you don't write that version first. You write the readable version, with real names joined in, so you can eyeball the data before committing to anything. Five real AdventureWorks2012 tables, joined together, nothing invented: SalesOrderHeader, SalesOrderDetail, SalesTerritory, Product, and ProductSubcategory.

Four of those joins are INNER JOIN, on purpose: every order line always has exactly one header, one territory, and one product, so an inner join never drops a row you need. But Product to ProductSubcategory is a LEFT JOIN, because a handful of products in AdventureWorks2012 have a NULL ProductSubcategoryID. An inner join there would silently drop those order lines. A LEFT JOIN keeps them, with the subcategory name showing NULL instead.

And the WHERE clause filters to Status equals 5, Shipped. Both stakeholders care about completed business. The Sales Director's totals shouldn't include an order that hasn't shipped yet, and the Operations Manager's fulfillment math only makes sense for orders that actually have a ship date to compare against a due date. Filter once, here, and every measure built later inherits the correct scope automatically.

Notice DueDate and ShipDate are pulled even though neither report page uses them yet. That's deliberate. The Operations Manager's drill-down page in Lesson 8 needs a fulfillment metric, and Lesson 15's change request depends on these exact two columns. Pulling them now, while you're already writing this query, is cheaper than coming back for them later.

Run this against AdventureWorks2012 and compare its row count to the COUNT from Lesson 2's grain-check query — they should match exactly. Next lesson: turning this query into a view, so it isn't retyped by hand every single week.
